out.other_title: By reducing the need for human feedback, constitutional methods make it easier to deploy AI systems not thoroughly tested and observed by humans
out.rationale: Bai et al. state that reducing the need for human feedback makes it easier to train and deploy AI systems not thoroughly tested and observed by humans, which could lead developers to deploy models with unforeseen failure modes. Goel et al. say their results indicate that as model blind-spots get harder to detect and humans defer more to AI oversight, models also make more similar mistakes, posing safety risks from correlated failures; they give this among potential implications if this trend continues.
out.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether replacing human feedback with AI oversight introduces new failure risks, for LLM judges and training on LM annotations

open_obligations: Check whether Choi et al.'s agents are samples from one model and, if so, whether correlated errors among them violate the independence assumption.
Note that Goel et al.'s passage concerns similarity across models; check whether it applies to repeated samples from one model.
Check Choi et al.'s condition that the correct answer is the most probable option.
out.other_title: Majority voting success probability approaches 1 as the number of agents grows
out.rationale: Choi, Zhu and Li prove majority voting succeeds with probability approaching 1 as N grows, assuming homogeneous independent agents whose top belief is on the correct answer. Goel et al. say that as model blind-spots get harder to detect, models also make more similar mistakes, and that if this trend continues it could undermine benefits from using LM juries by compromising independence; Goel et al.'s passage concerns similar mistakes across models, while Choi et al.'s agents share homogeneous initial beliefs, so the challenge is to the independence assumption in practice.
out.scope: proposed CHALLENGES: whether adding more LLM voters reliably drives majority-vote accuracy toward 1

text: The authors argue that if the trend continues it could mean greater affinity bias in LM judges, lower gains from inter-LM training, and weaker benefits from LM juries through compromised independence and amplified collective biases; most concerningly, they say their results indicate that as model blind spots get harder to detect and humans defer more to AI oversight, models also make more similar mistakes, posing safety risks from correlated failures.
title: Correlated failures risk: deferring to AI oversight as model blind spots converge
